new.title: git grep invoked with context flag after pathspec and a pathspec placed before `--`, failing with exit 128
new.cause: The agent appends `-A12` after the pattern and path, and writes `git grep -n PATTERN crates/ -- ':!*/tests/*'`. Git treats the path before `--` as a revision, so it reports 'unable to resolve revision: crates/'. Git also requires options to come before non-option arguments. The failure aborts the compound command, so the intended code read does not happen. Rewriting would need git grep's argument grammar, which is: options, then the pattern, then optional revisions, then `--`, then pathspecs.

verdict.severity_reason: Contained and self-correcting: the command fails loudly with exit 128 and the agent retries with the right order, costing one wasted call.
verdict.reason: The failure is real git behavior: `git grep` takes options first, then the pattern, then revisions, then `--`, then pathspecs. The codebook already records many near-identical sightings (for example around lines 30907, 31350, 31406 and 32331 of docs/legibility/confusion-codebook.yaml), so this one is a repeat. But the cause is the agent's habit with git/GNU grep argument order, which is tooling this tree does not contain. No existing tree file teaches the wrong form. My search for `git grep` with `-A` or `crates/ --` found hits only in the confusion-census plans and the codebook, which are records of the mistake, not instructions that teach it. Mentioning that the tree's CLAUDE.md already recommends the Grep tool or `git grep` is not a cause of the confusion either.

new.title: Post-merge gui-script verification fails on a cold cargo registry, and the remediation is blocked by Bash permission denial
new.cause: test_run_gui_scripts.sh fails during post-merge verification because cargo cannot resolve reify-gui and tauri on a cold registry. The failure message prescribes warming the registry (cargo fetch --locked or scripts/setup-dev.sh), but the autonomous don't-ask-mode session denies Bash, so the agent cannot run the prescribed fix or inspect the registry. The failure is environmental yet is reported as a test_failure, which makes it hard to distinguish from a code regression.

verdict.severity_reason: The failure is contained to one infra test whose message already names the likely fix. The cost is only an agent mistaking an environmental failure for a code regression.
verdict.reason: The quoted FAIL line is still emitted by `_t36_resolve` in tests/infra/test_run_gui_scripts.sh. Its label prescribes `cargo fetch --locked` or scripts/setup-dev.sh. `_rgs_tauri_features_under` runs `cargo metadata --locked --offline` with stderr sent to /dev/null and returns a bare 1 on any failure. A cold registry therefore looks the same as a real resolve regression, such as a Cargo.lock drift or a feature typo. The assertion gives no way to tell an environmental cause from a code one. The Bash-denial half of the cluster comes from the session's permission tooling, which this tree does not contain, so I could not verify it.
verdict.proposal: In `_rgs_tauri_features_under`, capture cargo metadata's stderr and use distinct return codes, or print the stderr tail, so a cold-registry or offline failure is distinguishable from a lock or feature resolve error, and let `_t36_resolve` report which one occurred.

new.observation: In one session the agent wrote `git grep -n PATTERN crates/ -- ':!*/tests/*'` with `-A12` appended after the pattern and path. Git read the path before `--` as a revision and exited 128 with 'unable to resolve revision: crates/', which aborted the compound command, so the intended code read did not happen. Under heuristic 10 (clear invariants, informatively, redundantly, uniformly enforced), the breach was loud and named the offending value, but the message does not state the argument order git expects: options, pattern, revisions, `--`, pathspecs. The verdict found no file in this tree that teaches the wrong form; the only hits were the census plans and codebook that record the mistake. The cost seen was one wasted call before the agent retried with the right order.

The assertion message in `workspace_module_sccs_match_the_committed_baseline` carries no inline explanation of GREW or STALE. It sends the reader to `python3 scripts/assert-module-scc.py --help` for their meaning and for how to lower a baseline row. Under heuristic 11 (SPOT — single point of truth), that explanation has one home and both the message and CLAUDE.md point at it; the verdict confirmed the pointer is accurate. Under heuristic 10 (clear invariants, informatively, redundantly, uniformly enforced), the red ratchet names the invariant, but its informative half is reachable only by executing the script. In the one session, Bash calls to the script were reported denied under don't-ask mode, leaving the agent without the documented fix path. That denial comes from the agent harness and could not be observed from the tree.

`_rgs_tauri_features_under` in `tests/infra/test_run_gui_scripts.sh` runs `cargo metadata --locked --offline` with stderr sent to /dev/null and returns a bare 1 on any failure. A cold registry is therefore indistinguishable from a real resolve regression such as Cargo.lock drift or a feature typo. Under heuristic 10 (clear invariants, informatively, redundantly, uniformly enforced), the FAIL line from `_t36_resolve` prescribes a remedy (`cargo fetch --locked` or `scripts/setup-dev.sh`) but drops the offending values that would say which cause occurred. Under heuristic 1 (informative names), the environmental failure surfaces as a `test_failure`, a label that reads as a code regression. In the one session this happened during post-merge verification, and the prescribed warm-up was reported blocked by a Bash permission denial. That denial comes from the session's permission tooling and was not verifiable from the tree.

phase_refinements.why: The verified part of the finding is in how the infra test helper is written: it discards cargo's stderr and collapses every failure to a bare return code. That places the origin in implementation of the test, where the stamp says unknown. The failure surfaced during post-merge verification, so the manifested phase is unchanged.

findings.statement: The agent chained several check scripts with their rc values echoed, then ran `tail -3` over more than one log file in a single call. GNU tail rejects the obsolete `-N` form when several files are given (`option used in invalid context -- 3`) and the Bash call exits 1. Every check had already reported rc=0, so the exit status contradicts the results. The agent must notice that the failure comes only from the trailing inspection step and then re-run it as `tail -n 3`. Verifier: The confusion comes from GNU tail's behavior (it rejects the obsolete `-N` form when given several files) in the agent's own ad-hoc Bash call. I searched /home/leo/src/reify/scripts for `tail -N` applied to several log files and found no match. I found no script, doc, or file in this tree that teaches or produces the pattern, so this is a tooling quirk that this tree does not cause.

The 'Re-arm L2 watcher (reify) in background' task is dispatched as a bounded background command that frequently exceeds its wait window (exit code 124) or gets killed outright; rather than the underlying timeout/lifetime mismatch being fixed, the agent's only recourse is to keep re-issuing the same re-arm command dozens of times across the whole session, producing a chronic churn loop instead of a stable watcher. Verifier: The re-arm mechanism is not in this tree. A glob for `watcher-rearm*` under /home/leo/src/reify finds no file. The only matches for 'Re-arm L2 watcher' are in docs/legibility/confusion-codebook.yaml, the plans/confusion-census-* files, and a few notes and PRDs that quote the phrase. The exit-124 timeouts and killed background tasks come from dark-factory's watcher and background-task tooling. Nothing in reify's current files produces or teaches the churn or fails to guard against it, so no observable fact about this tree is confirmed. The codebook only records past sightings of the same pattern.

Once mcp__escalation__get_pending_escalations/get_escalation calls begin returning 'The operation timed out', the autonomous watcher reissues the identical call with identical params on later turns rather than recognizing the endpoint as wedged, backing off, or surfacing the failure — burning turns/escalation budget until the supervisor's rotation limit (ROTATION_ESCALATIONS/ROTATION_HOURS) forces an exit with no escalations actually handled. Verifier: The reify tree contains no escalation-watcher prompt, MCP escalation server, or retry logic. The only mentions of get_pending_escalations and ROTATION_ESCALATIONS are in confusion-codebook and census records (docs/legibility/confusion-codebook.yaml, plans/confusion-census-*), which log earlier sightings of this behaviour. They do not show it in the current code. The watcher's retry behaviour and the escalation server's timeouts are in dark-factory tooling that this tree does not contain, so the claim can't be confirmed as a current fact about this tree.

The watcher's 'bounded foreground wait for new L1' subprocess call (uv run escalation.watcher --timeout 540, wrapped in a Bash tool call with timeout=560000) exits 137 (killed) rather than completing normally or timing out cleanly. The agent has no signal to distinguish 'subprocess was killed' from 'no new escalation arrived within the wait window', so it re-issues the exact same command with the same --exclude-id 25 times in a row rather than switching to a backgrounded run, shortening the wait slice, or escalating the repeated kill as a systemic problem. Verifier: The watcher (`escalation.watcher`) and the agent loop that calls it are in dark-factory, not in this tree. The only matches in /home/leo/src/reify are the codebook and census files, which record earlier sightings of the same pattern. Nothing under reify's source or docs produces, teaches or fails to guard against the repeated exit-137 retries. I also can't observe the SIGKILL cause, so no current-state fact can be confirmed here.

An autonomous escalation-watcher rotation (reify, 4h/50-escalation limits) hit the same class of ModuleNotFoundError at three distinct turns (21, 27, 44), indicating a missing/broken Python dependency in the watcher's execution environment that was never resolved and instead recurred across separate escalation-handling attempts within one session. Verifier: I can't confirm this as an observable fact about the reify tree. The claim is about an escalation-watcher session's Python environment, which is dark-factory tooling outside this tree. Nothing under /home/leo/src/reify contains or configures that watcher's interpreter or venv. The only trace in reify is the codebook, which records earlier ModuleNotFoundError sightings (e.g. cand-20260724-5, cand-20260724-18) as rejected env-mismatch candidates. Those involve bare python outside dark-factory's uv venv, which is a runtime environment issue. No existing reify file produces or teaches the confusion, so I can't name a remediation.

When a type was renamed, the editing agent substituted the new name into an existing list of main.rs-private helpers without checking its actual visibility. The type is public in the library module, so the brief would have told the downstream implementer to move a library type out of main.rs. Verifier: The claim no longer holds in the current tree. `DebugServerSlot` is public in the library module `gui/src-tauri/src/debug_server_slot.rs`, and `main.rs` imports it from `reify_gui::debug_server_slot`. The PRD brief `docs/prds/v0_6/gui-frontend-wire-bindings-bridge-port.md` (lines 134-137 and 292) no longer lists it among the main.rs-private items. It says the type is the library's managed `debug_server_slot::DebugServerSlot`, which "needs no move", and that it "stays in the library's debug_server_slot module, not moved". The stale visibility claim was corrected, so nothing in the tree still teaches the confusion.

The plan assumed the parse guard was the only test that reads every tracked .ri file. The shared corpus listing in tracked_corpus.rs is used by every repo-wide .ri sweep in the test binary, and the agent did not check its other call sites before narrowing the change. Verifier: The confusion was a past planning error, not a current defect in the tree. `crates/reify-syntax/tests/common/tracked_corpus.rs` opens by saying every repo-wide `.ri` sweep in the binary reads `swept_ri_paths`. Both known consumers, `member_continuation_ambiguity_tests.rs` and `tracked_ri_parse_guard.rs`, import from it. The omission list `VERIFY_INERT_RI_TREES` is held equal to the scope classifier by `is_verify_inert_agrees_with_the_scope_classifier`. The warning already sits where an agent would read it, and the tree has no misleading single-consumer claim.
